justice: Complete absence of paved sidewalks on the right side severely limits accessibility for wheelchair users and persons with mobility disabilities.
Space distribution heavily favors motorized vehicles with multiple wide lanes, reflecting poor spatial equity for active transport users.
Lack of tactile paving or safe roadside paths creates unfair, discriminatory conditions for visually impaired pedestrians navigating this area.
safety: Absence of separated bike lanes forces cyclists to share the road with high-speed motorized traffic, significantly increasing collision risks.
Lack of pedestrian sidewalks forces people to walk on the roadway or uneven dirt shoulder, creating severe safety hazards for all age groups.
Wide, straight vehicular lanes without traffic calming measures encourage speeding, endangering teenagers and elderly road users.
livability: Absence of commercial storefronts, residential entrances, or community amenities makes the environment sterile and uninviting for daily activities.
No street furniture such as benches or resting areas are provided along the roadside, severely reducing usability for older adults needing breaks.
Lack of visible pedestrian activity or social spaces limits community vitality and eliminates passive safety surveillance (eyes on the street).
sustainability: Presence of unpaved soil and grass buffers along the roadside allows for natural rainwater infiltration and reduces runoff.
Young street trees planted along the verge offer future green infrastructure, though their current ecological and shading benefits are minimal.
Lack of dedicated public transit stops or active transport infrastructure fails to encourage low-carbon travel alternatives.
aesthetics: The street surface is visually clean with freshly painted yellow lane markings and no visible litter or debris.
Trees planted uniformly along both sides of the road provide a basic sense of visual rhythm and natural greenery.
The environment feels monotonous and barren due to the complete lack of architectural variety, public art, or varied landscape design.
comfort: Young, sparsely foliaged street trees provide almost no shade, leading to poor thermal comfort for pedestrians or cyclists in hot weather.
The uneven dirt and grass on the roadside offer terrible physical comfort for walking, especially for older adults or those using mobility aids.
Proximity to fast-moving multi-lane traffic without a physical barrier creates high psychological discomfort and excessive noise stress.
walkability: There are absolutely no paved sidewalks provided on the near side, making basic walking along this corridor nearly impossible.
No safe pedestrian crossings, crosswalks, or curb ramps are visible in the immediate foreground, destroying route connectivity.
The harsh, car-dominated environment offers zero pedestrian-scale lighting or shading to encourage walking for any social group.
bikeability: No dedicated or protected bicycle lanes exist, forcing cyclists to navigate wide, unprotected vehicle lanes.
Lack of bicycle parking facilities or clear cycling signage reduces the convenience and perceived legitimacy of bike travel.
The high-speed road design without physical barriers creates extremely intimidating conditions for adolescent and elderly cyclists.
